habitat: Wild from Newfoundland and Manitoba through the Great Lakes and New England, and south along the Appalachians to northern Georgia. It grows on almost any soil, but competes best on well-drained sands and gravels, where it once formed vast stands; it also takes rocky ridges and the edges of bogs. Young trees grow well in partial shade.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the central United States, from Pennsylvania west to South Dakota and south to Texas, mostly on the rich, moist bottomlands of river valleys and on limestone soils. Planted, it puts up with drought, road salt, compacted soil and city heat, which is how it reached northern streets.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The most widespread oak of the Northeast, from Nova Scotia and the Great Lakes south to Alabama and west to Minnesota and eastern Oklahoma. It grows best on deep, moist, well-drained loams on north- and east-facing slopes and in coves, but is common on drier ridges too. Its seedlings stand moderate shade and shoot up when a gap opens in the canopy.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild along rivers, streams and the edges of swamps in the eastern and central United States, from southern New England and New York to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas, on ground that floods in spring. It needs sun, and acid soil: on alkaline ground its leaves turn yellow.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across much of Europe, from Norway and Finland south to northern Spain and Greece and east to the Caucasus, in mixed forests on rich, moist soils, seldom in stands of its own. In North American woods its seedlings stand deep shade, and come up thickly under its own crown.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: A tree of wet ground: river bottoms, the edges of swamps and lakes, and flats that flood in spring, from southern Quebec and Maine west to Minnesota and south to Missouri and Virginia, scattered among other trees rather than in stands. In Vermont it grows wild mostly in the lowland forests of the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild only in the central and southern Rocky Mountains, from Wyoming and Idaho to New Mexico and Arizona, mostly along streams and on moist slopes in mountain valleys between about 6,000 and 11,000 feet, seldom in stands of its own. Planted, it does best in full sun and well-drained soil.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: It grows on a wider range of ground than almost any other tree in eastern North America: swamps and stream banks, dry rocky ridges and everything between, in sun or part shade, from Newfoundland to Florida and west to Minnesota and eastern Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in scattered mountain ranges of southern Europe and Asia Minor, from Spain and Corsica through Austria and the Balkans to Crimea and Turkey, often on limestone and on poor, dry, rocky soils where few other trees do well.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild on poorly drained bottomlands and flats that stand in water through winter and spring, from southern New England and New York west to Iowa and Kansas and south to Tennessee and North Carolina. It needs acid soil, and grows fast in full sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec west to Minnesota and south to Tennessee, and along the Appalachians to Georgia. At its best on deep, moist, fertile, well-drained loams, where it often dominates the forest with beech and yellow birch. Its seedlings stand deep shade and can wait decades under the canopy for a gap.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and the St. Lawrence west to Manitoba, and south through the Great Lakes states and New England, with scattered outliers in the Appalachians. It grows in two very different places: cedar swamps on wet, often limy peat, and dry limestone ledges and cliffs.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: One of the most widespread trees in North America: across the northern forest from Newfoundland and Labrador to Alaska, and south to the Great Lakes, northern New England and the Adirondacks. It grows on a wide range of soils, best on moist, well-drained loams, and stands bitter cold.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across most of Europe, from England and Spain east to the Urals and the Caucasus, in mixed broadleaf forests on fertile soils. In England it is a mark of ancient woodland, where it has grown since before people cleared the land.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in the mountains of central and southeastern Europe, up to about 2,000 m in the Alps, and across the lowlands of Scandinavia and northern Russia, where it forms vast forests on cool, moist soils.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in Japan, Korea, eastern China and Taiwan, along streams and in moist valleys on rich soils.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Almost every ginkgo alive was planted. Whether any truly wild ones remain is debated: the likeliest are scattered trees in the mountains of southwestern China, which some think were kept alive by Buddhist monks for centuries.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild from New Brunswick west to Manitoba and south to Arkansas and the mountains of North Carolina, on moist, deep, fertile soils of slopes and valleys. It grows mixed with sugar maple, elms and ashes rather than in stands, and sprouts readily from a cut stump.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: A tree of riverbanks and floodplains, from New Brunswick west to Minnesota and south to Louisiana and Georgia, where it stands spring floods for weeks. In Vermont it dominates the floodplain forests along the big rivers and the shores of Lake Champlain.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Across the northern forest from Newfoundland to Alaska, south to Pennsylvania and the Great Lakes. A pioneer: it seeds into ground opened by fire, logging or clearing, in full sun, and gives way in time to trees that stand more shade.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Quebec and Maine west to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas, along streams, in bottomlands and on rich lower slopes, in the shade of taller hardwoods. It stands more shade than almost any tree it grows among.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Native to the eastern United States, chiefly the Southeast and the lower Midwest, at forest edges, in old fields and thickets and in young woods coming back on cleared land. In New England, Vermont included, it grows only where planted.
source: Go Botany (Native Plant Trust)

habitat: Wild in northern Japan, mostly Hokkaido, and in Korea, northern China and the far southeast of Russia, in mixed forests, valleys and gullies from near sea level into the mountains.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild from southern Maine west to Iowa and Nebraska and south to northern Florida and Texas, almost always on bottomlands and along streams, where it grows faster than nearly any hardwood. It is often among the first trees on new ground left by a river.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Its original range is not known exactly: two separate areas, one in the Appalachians from Pennsylvania and southern Ohio to Alabama and Georgia, the other in the Ozarks and Ouachita Mountains of Missouri, Arkansas and Oklahoma. Planted for posts and erosion control, it has since run wild across the country and into Europe and Asia, on open, disturbed ground in full sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild only in a few mountain ranges of the Balkans: mainly the Pindus of Greece, with small stands in North Macedonia, Albania and Bulgaria, in moist, shaded ravines and valley forests. The trees of streets and parks across Europe and North America all descend from planted ones.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Wild across most of Europe, from Ireland and Portugal east to the Urals and the Caucasus, at its best on deep, moist, fertile soils, including heavy clays and river floodplains. It needs sun: its seedlings fail under a closed canopy.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild on the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from Delaware to Florida and Texas, and up the Mississippi valley to southern Illinois and Indiana, in swamps, river bottoms and lake edges that stand in water for much of the year. Planted in the open it does well on ordinary soil, and is hardy far north of where it grows wild.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Across the central and northern plains and the Midwest, from southern Manitoba and New Brunswick south to Texas, farther west than any other eastern oak: on river bottoms, dry uplands and the savannas between forest and prairie, where its thick bark let it survive the grass fires that kept other trees out. In Vermont it grows wild in the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the mountains of northern Japan, mostly Hokkaido and northern Honshu, and in Korea, Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and the far southeast of Russia: the coldest homeland of any of the ornamental cherries.
source: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

habitat: A cultivated form that grows wild nowhere, kept going from cuttings. Its species, the black poplar, grows wild along rivers and on floodplains from Europe to central Asia, on wet sand and gravel that floods.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Native to a small area of the central Mississippi valley, from southern Illinois and Indiana to Arkansas and western Tennessee, in bottomland woods along streams and at the foot of bluffs. Planted far beyond that for its flowers and fast growth, it has run wild in old fields and along fencerows across much of the East.
source: Missouri Department of Conservation

habitat: Before the blight it was among the commonest trees of the Appalachian forest, from Maine and southern Ontario to Georgia and Mississippi, above all on well-drained, acid soils of ridges and upper slopes. It survives there now mostly as sprouts from old root systems.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in two forms: the coast Douglas fir, from British Columbia to central California, among the tallest trees in the world; and the smaller, hardier Rocky Mountain Douglas fir, from Alberta to Mexico. The trees planted in the Northeast are mostly the inland form, which stands cold winters.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Scotland and Spain across Europe and northern Asia to eastern Siberia, and north beyond the Arctic Circle in Scandinavia. It grows on a wide range of soils, including dry sands and poor, rocky ground where little else does well, but needs full sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Scattered through the hardwood forests of the East and Midwest, from western Vermont and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, rarely in stands of its own. It grows best on deep, rich, moist but well-drained bottomlands and coves, and needs sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Michigan and New Jersey south to Florida, and west to Texas and northern Mexico, mostly as a small understory tree of open woods, woodland edges, rocky slopes and stream banks.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild through almost the whole of the eastern United States, from southern Maine and Quebec west to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas, on many kinds of ground but best on deep, moist, well-drained soils. It is long-lived, slow-growing and moderately shade-tolerant.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and the Great Lakes south along the Appalachians to Georgia and Alabama, in cool, moist places: ravines, north-facing slopes, stream banks and rocky ridges. It stands more shade than almost any other tree in its range.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern New England and southern Ontario west to Michigan and south to Florida and Louisiana, at its best in the deep, moist, well-drained soils of Appalachian coves and lower slopes. It grows fast and needs sun, so it fills gaps and old fields. In Vermont it is rare.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from Hungary and the Balkans to western Turkey, in mixed broadleaf forests on lowlands and hills. Its tolerance of heat and dry summers comes from there.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild only in a small area of central China, on the borders of Hubei, Hunan and Chongqing, in valleys and along streams in the mountains, mostly in or beside rice paddies and villages. Very few of the wild trees remain.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild from Connecticut and southern Illinois south to Florida and Texas, with scattered stands in the mountains of Mexico and Central America. A tree of bottomlands and moist slopes, it also seeds fast into old fields and cutover land.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Across the East from Nova Scotia and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, on rich, moist, well-drained soils, often with sugar maple and yellow birch in the northern hardwood forest. It stands deep shade, and spreads by suckers from its roots into thickets of young beech.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Europe across the Caucasus and the Himalaya to central China, on dry, rocky, sunny hillsides and in open woods, often on limestone.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild across most of Europe, north to southern Scandinavia, and in North Africa and western Asia, in woods, woodland edges and old hedgerows, on chalk and limestone as well as heavy clays.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: An understory tree of dry, well-drained slopes and ridges across the East, from Nova Scotia and Manitoba to Florida and Texas, with stands in the mountains of Mexico and Central America. It grows slowly in the shade of oaks and maples.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild along the Pacific coast from southern Alaska to northern California, and inland in the Cascades, in cool, wet mountain forests, mostly at middle and upper elevations. It stands deep snow and poor, wet soils.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec west to Minnesota and south through the Appalachians, on sandy and gravelly uplands. It needs full sun and comes in fast after fire or cutting, mostly by suckers from the roots of the trees that were there.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the lower Midwest and the upper South, from Pennsylvania west to Kansas and south to Tennessee and Arkansas, on moist bottomlands and slopes, and in old fields and open woods.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild from Newfoundland and southern Quebec west to Minnesota, and south along the Appalachians to Georgia, on cool, moist, well-drained soils of slopes and stream banks, with sugar maple, beech and hemlock in the northern hardwood forest. Its seedlings take root on rotting logs and mossy stumps.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec to Pennsylvania and New Jersey, on poor, dry, sandy or gravelly ground and in abandoned fields, where it is among the first trees to come in after fire or clearing.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in the eastern United States from New Jersey and Ohio south to Florida and Texas, as a small understory tree of moist woods, stream banks and the edges of swamps, and on dry rocky bluffs.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in Japan and China, in moist forests along mountain streams, where old trees grow to great size, often with several trunks.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild across most of Europe, from southern England and Sweden to Sicily and the Balkans, forming forests of its own on well-drained soils, especially chalk and limestone. Its dense shade keeps almost anything else from growing beneath it.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in China, Korea and Taiwan, in thickets, on forest edges and in mountain woods. Planted across North America, it has run wild in old fields, roadsides and woodland edges in much of the East.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild but scattered and nowhere common, from western New York and southern Ontario to Nebraska and Oklahoma, mostly on rich, moist bottomlands and lower slopes. It spreads by suckers, so a stand is often one tree's clones.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in Japan, Korea and China, in mountain forests and thickets, as a small understory tree.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: A cultivated tree, found wild only where it has escaped. Its main ancestor, the wild apple Malus sieversii, still grows in the mountain forests of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, in the Tian Shan.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild in the mountains of northeastern China and Korea, in mixed forests on slopes and along streams.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: The most widespread maple in North America, wild from New England and southern Canada to Florida, California and Guatemala. A tree of riverbanks, floodplains and lake shores that also seeds fast into vacant lots, rail yards and old fields.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from West Virginia south to Florida and west to Arkansas and Oklahoma, along streams and on moist, rich slopes in coves.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, as an understory tree of open hardwood and pine forests, on moist, well-drained, acid soils. In Vermont it grows wild only in the south of the state.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Rare and scattered in the wild, in a few counties from Kentucky and Tennessee to Arkansas and Alabama, mostly on limestone cliffs, ridges and the rich soils of coves and stream banks.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild only in central China, in mixed forests on mountain slopes, where it is now rare.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild from southern Quebec and western Vermont to the Dakotas and south to Oklahoma and Georgia, most often on river bottoms and floodplains but also on dry, rocky limestone ridges. In Vermont it grows wild mostly in the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in northeastern China, Korea, Japan and the Russian Far East, in mixed forests along rivers and on mountain slopes. Planted in the Northeast, it seeds into nearby woods.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: The most widespread ash in North America, wild from Nova Scotia to Alberta and south to Florida and Texas, on moist bottomlands and stream banks. Planted along streets across the continent, it is now dying everywhere the emerald ash borer has reached.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the mountain forests of Japan and Korea, in moist, rich soils, often near streams.
source: Wikipedia

habitat: Wild across almost all of Europe and northern Asia, from Iceland and Spain to Siberia, higher in the mountains than almost any other broadleaf tree. It grows on thin, acid soils, rocky ground and the edges of woods.
source: Wikipedia
